title: Imports & paths
summary: Bring names into scope with use; paths locate items in modules or crates.
rules: crate starts at this crate’s root; self is the current module; super is its parent.
Use as to rename a binding, braces to group paths, and * for a glob import. Visibility still applies.
pub use re-exports a name. A use declaration does not install a dependency.

title: Functions & return values
summary: A function declares typed parameters and an optional return type; its body is an expression block.
rules: Parameters require types; an omitted return type means (). The final expression without a semicolon supplies the return value.
return exits early. Functions returning ! never complete normally.
Functions can have generics, where bounds, visibility, and async, const, unsafe, or extern qualifiers.

title: Modules & visibility
summary: Modules organize items and control which names other modules can access.
rules: Items are private by default; descendants can access ancestor-private items. pub exposes an item through accessible paths.
mod name; loads a file module, normally name.rs or name/mod.rs. use introduces names without declaring a module.
pub(crate), pub(super), and pub(in path) restrict visibility; the path must name an ancestor module.

title: Constants & statics
summary: Constants are values substituted at use sites; statics identify a single storage location.
rules: const and static require explicit types and compile-time initializers. Constants need not have a unique address.
Shared statics require Sync. Prefer atomics or synchronization primitives for shared mutable state.
static mut exists but accessing it is unsafe; creating references to mutable statics is denied by default in edition 2024.

title: Bindings, mutability & shadowing
summary: let binds a value using a pattern. Bindings are immutable unless marked mut.
rules: Use a type annotation when inference is insufficient. mut permits reassignment or mutable borrowing.
A new let with the same name shadows the earlier binding and may change its type.
Ordinary let patterns must be irrefutable. let-else accepts a refutable pattern but its else branch must diverge.

title: Ownership & moves
summary: Each value has an owner; leaving the owner’s scope drops the value unless ownership was transferred.
rules: Assignment, passing an argument, and returning a value move non-Copy values. The moved binding can no longer be read.
Borrow with & or &mut to use a value without transferring ownership.
A move can be partial for eligible structs; fields already moved cannot be accessed and the whole value cannot be used.

title: Shared references
summary: A shared reference borrows access to a value without becoming its owner.
rules: Multiple shared references can coexist. While a shared borrow is active, ordinary mutation through another reference is forbidden.
A reference must not outlive its referent. Dereferencing a shared reference cannot move a non-Copy value out of it.
Methods often auto-borrow and auto-dereference. Interior-mutability types provide controlled mutation through shared references.

title: Mutable references
summary: A mutable reference gives exclusive access for the duration of its borrow.
rules: A live mutable borrow excludes other accesses that conflict with it, including shared borrows of the same data.
The binding of the referent must allow mutation. The &mut reference itself need not be a mut binding to mutate its referent.
Reborrowing temporarily lends access from an existing reference; disjoint fields or slice splitting can allow independent borrows.

title: Copy & Clone
summary: Copy permits implicit duplication; Clone provides an explicit duplication operation.
rules: Copy requires Clone and every field to be Copy; a type implementing Drop cannot be Copy.
Clone may allocate or run arbitrary logic. String and Vec are Clone but not Copy.
Cloning Rc or Arc duplicates a shared ownership handle rather than the underlying value.

title: String & str
summary: str is UTF-8 text, usually borrowed as &str; String owns a growable UTF-8 buffer.
rules: len reports bytes. Use chars for Unicode scalar values and bytes for raw bytes; neither counts user-perceived graphemes.
String does not support integer character indexing. String slices must lie on UTF-8 boundaries; get returns None for invalid boundaries.
&String coerces to &str. Prefer &str for functions that only read text.

title: Slices & ranges
summary: A slice is a dynamically sized view into contiguous elements, carried by a reference.
rules: Ranges exclude their upper bound unless written ..=. Indexing and slicing panic when out of bounds.
Use get or get_mut for checked access. &[T] permits shared reads; &mut [T] permits exclusive mutation.
split_at_mut produces disjoint mutable slices; it panics if the split position exceeds the length.

title: Option<T>
summary: Option represents either a value, Some(T), or its absence, None.
rules: Use match, if let, or combinators to handle absence. unwrap and expect panic on None.
? returns None early from an Option-returning function or compatible context.
as_ref and as_mut borrow the contained value. take replaces the option with None; replace stores a new value and returns the old one.

title: Result<T, E>
summary: Result separates successful output Ok(T) from a recoverable error Err(E).
rules: ? propagates Err early, converting errors through From when needed. It unwraps Ok for continued work.
unwrap and expect panic on Err. Use match, combinators, or ? for recoverable failures.
as_ref borrows both variants. ok discards errors; err discards successful output.

title: Patterns & match
summary: Patterns destructure values and choose branches; match must cover all possible values.
rules: Arms use pattern => expression; guards add boolean conditions. Guarded arms do not establish exhaustive coverage.
_ ignores a value, .. ignores remaining fields or elements, | offers alternatives, and @ binds a matched value.
Patterns can move, copy, or borrow bindings depending on the scrutinee and binding mode. Match ergonomics change some explicit ref/mut rules in edition 2024.

title: Struct forms
summary: Structs group fields into named, tuple, or unit-shaped types.
rules: Named fields use dot access; tuple fields use numeric positions. Fields are private unless declared pub.
Field shorthand uses a variable with the same name. Update syntax moves or copies omitted fields from the base value.
Methods and associated functions live in impl blocks. A struct definition can include type and lifetime parameters.

title: Enums & variants
summary: An enum defines a type with a finite set of variants, each optionally carrying data.
rules: Qualify variants with the enum name unless imported. Variants may be unit, tuple, or struct shaped.
Use match or if let to access variant data. Exhaustive matching helps detect newly added variants.

title: impl, methods & associated functions
summary: impl blocks attach behavior to a type. Methods have a self receiver; associated functions do not.
rules: Self names the implementing type. self takes ownership, &self borrows, and &mut self borrows exclusively.
Inherent impl blocks can define associated constants and multiple methods; trait impl blocks implement a named trait.
Method calls perform automatic borrowing and dereferencing where applicable. Visibility is private by default.

title: Traits & implementations
summary: Traits describe shared behavior through methods, associated types, and associated constants.
rules: Supertraits require implementations of their parent traits. Defaults can be overridden.
Generic bounds use static dispatch; dyn uses a trait object and requires a dyn-compatible trait.
Coherence limits implementations: typically the trait or a participating type must be local, and overlapping implementations are forbidden.

title: Generic parameters & bounds
summary: Generic definitions abstract over types, lifetimes, and const values.
rules: Bounds restrict allowed types. Multiple bounds use +; where clauses can constrain complex types.
Type arguments are often inferred. Use ::<...> on expression paths to supply them explicitly.
Type parameters are Sized by default; ?Sized relaxes that implicit bound. Defaults are allowed in some type and trait declarations, not function type parameters.

title: Lifetime relationships
summary: Lifetimes express how long references remain valid and how borrowed inputs relate to outputs.
rules: Annotations describe relationships; they do not extend a value’s life. Returning references to local owned values is invalid.
Elision handles common signatures. A receiver’s lifetime normally determines an elided returned reference lifetime.
'static on a reference means the referent can live for the program; T: 'static means T contains no shorter-lived borrowed references.

title: Iterator basics
summary: An Iterator yields Option<Item> from next; adapters build pipelines and consumers drive them.
rules: iter borrows, iter_mut borrows exclusively, and into_iter consumes its receiver; references can also implement IntoIterator.
Adapters such as map and filter are lazy. collect, for_each, fold, and for loops consume items.
Iterator methods often take self and move the iterator. by_ref temporarily borrows an iterator for a sub-pipeline.

title: Closure syntax & captures
summary: Closures are anonymous functions that may capture variables from their enclosing scope.
rules: Captures are inferred as shared borrow, mutable borrow, or move. move forces captured ownership into the closure.
FnOnce can consume captures; FnMut may mutate them; Fn can be called through a shared reference. One closure can implement several call traits.
Async closures require Rust 1.85+. Parameter and return types are usually inferred from usage.

title: Vec<T>
summary: Vec owns a growable sequence of contiguous elements of one type.
rules: push appends; pop returns Option<T>. Indexing panics on invalid indices; get returns None.
Length is the number of initialized elements; capacity is allocated space. Growth may reallocate and invalidate raw pointers.
Vec coerces to slices for borrowed access. Repetition clones the supplied value.

title: HashMap<K, V>
summary: HashMap associates unique keys with values using hashing.
rules: Keys require Eq and Hash. insert returns the old value if the key was already present.
get and get_mut borrow keys and return optional references. entry supports a single lookup for insert-or-update.
Iteration order is unspecified. Use BTreeMap when sorted iteration or key ranges are required.

title: Loops, labels & exits
summary: Rust has unconditional, conditional, and iterator loops, plus labeled blocks for early exits.
rules: loop repeats until broken; while checks its condition before each iteration; for uses IntoIterator.
break exits a loop and continue starts its next iteration; labels select an enclosing loop. Labeled blocks support break but not continue.
Only loop and labeled blocks can return a non-unit break value. while and for evaluate to (). Ranges with .. exclude the endpoint; ..= includes it.

title: Async & await
summary: async creates a future; await suspends the current async computation until another future completes.
rules: Calling an async function creates a future rather than immediately running its body. An executor must poll the future.
await is allowed in async contexts. Rust’s standard library does not supply an application runtime; Tokio is one option.
async move takes ownership of captured values. Futures sent between threads may need Send; spawned tasks often require owned data with a static lifetime.

title: Tests & assertions
summary: The test harness finds functions marked #[test]; cfg(test) includes test-only code.
rules: Run cargo test. Unit tests can access private ancestor items; integration tests in tests/ use the public crate API.
#[ignore] skips a test unless requested. Tests may also return Result<(), E> to propagate failures.
Assertions remain active in release builds; debug_assert variants depend on debug assertions.

title: Derived implementations
summary: derive generates implementations of supported traits for structs and enums.
rules: Derives generally require the corresponding traits on fields; generated bounds can also constrain generic parameters.
Common built-in derives include Debug, Clone, Copy, Default, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord, and Hash.
Third-party derives are procedural macros and require the crate and its relevant features, such as serde’s derive feature.

title: Box, Rc & Arc
summary: Smart pointers manage ownership or storage while exposing pointer-like access.
rules: Box owns one heap allocation. Rc shares ownership within one thread; Arc uses atomic reference counts for sharing across threads.
Shared ownership does not itself permit mutation. Combine with RefCell, Mutex, or RwLock as appropriate.
Deref supports pointer-like method access. Reference cycles of strong Rc/Arc handles leak; use Weak for back-links.

title: Interior mutability
summary: Interior-mutability wrappers permit controlled mutation through a shared reference.
rules: Cell moves or copies values without returning ordinary references. get requires Copy.
RefCell enforces shared-versus-exclusive borrowing at runtime; borrow methods panic on conflicts while try_borrow methods return errors.
Cell and RefCell are not Sync. Use locks or atomics for synchronized cross-thread access.

title: Conversions & parsing
summary: Use conversion traits and parsing for semantic conversions; as handles a narrower set of casts.
rules: From/Into are infallible conversions; TryFrom/TryInto return Result. parse uses FromStr.
as numeric casts can truncate or change representation. Use checked conversions when loss would be an error.
to_string requires Display. Borrowing conversions such as AsRef avoid transferring ownership.

title: Numeric types & literals
summary: Rust has fixed-width signed and unsigned integers, pointer-sized integers, and floating-point types.
rules: Integer widths are 8, 16, 32, 64, and 128 bits; isize/usize match the target pointer width. Floats are f32 and f64.
Unsuffixed integers normally default to i32 and floats to f64 when unconstrained. Underscores separate digits.
Overflow behavior depends on operation and build checks. checked_ returns Option, wrapping_ wraps, saturating_ clamps, and overflowing_ also reports overflow.

title: Tuples & unit
summary: Tuples group a fixed number of values whose types may differ; () is the empty tuple.
rules: Tuple fields use zero-based numeric access. Destructuring patterns can ignore fields with _ or .. where allowed.
A one-element tuple needs a trailing comma; (value) is only grouping.
Functions without a return annotation return (); statements such as assignment also evaluate to unit.

title: Arrays
summary: An array owns a fixed-length sequence of elements of one type; its length is part of its type.
rules: The length must be a compile-time constant. Arrays coerce to borrowed slices when the length need not be part of an interface.
Repeated [value; count] forms usually require Copy; inline const blocks allow certain non-Copy repeated initializations.
Indexing panics out of bounds. get returns an Option, and iteration may borrow or consume the array.

title: if, if let & let-else
summary: Conditional expressions choose a branch and may produce a value.
rules: Conditions must be bool rather than truthy values. Branches of a value-producing if must have compatible types.
if let tests a pattern. let-else introduces bindings into the following scope and requires a diverging else branch.
Let chains with && require Rust 1.88+ and edition 2024; || does not combine let-pattern operands.

title: Formatting syntax
summary: Formatting macros interpret a checked format string and use formatting traits for arguments.
rules: {} uses Display; {:?} uses Debug; {:#?} pretty-prints Debug. Named captures and positional arguments are supported.
Width, alignment, precision, sign, padding, and base modifiers refine output. Escape braces by doubling them.
format! allocates a String; write! writes to a destination implementing the relevant fmt::Write or io::Write trait.

title: Unicode & UTF-8
summary: Rust char is a Unicode scalar value; strings are valid UTF-8 byte sequences.
rules: A char is not a grapheme cluster: a visible character can contain several scalar values.
String offsets are bytes; slicing must respect scalar boundaries. char_indices gives byte offsets for each scalar.
Grapheme segmentation and full Unicode normalization require dedicated libraries; chars alone provides neither.

title: Splitting & trimming text
summary: String splitting returns borrowed substrings using a pattern or predicate.
rules: split retains empty fields; split_whitespace skips whitespace runs. split_once returns an optional pair.
splitn limits the number of pieces; rsplit and rsplitn traverse from the right.
trim removes surrounding whitespace; strip_prefix/strip_suffix remove a specific match and return Option<&str>. lines handles line endings without retaining them.

title: HashSet<T>
summary: A set stores unique values and supports membership and set operations.
rules: HashSet requires Eq and Hash and has unspecified iteration order. insert returns whether the value was newly added.
Set-operation iterators borrow their inputs. symmetric_difference yields elements present in exactly one input.
Use BTreeSet for sorted traversal and range queries.

title: BTreeMap & BTreeSet
summary: Ordered collections store keys or values in sorted order according to Ord.
rules: BTreeMap has unique keys; BTreeSet has unique values. Both iterate in sorted order.
Range bounds may be included, excluded, or unbounded. Invalid bound combinations can panic.
Borrowed lookup keys must order consistently with the stored key representation.

title: Deque & priority queue
summary: VecDeque supports both ends of a sequence; BinaryHeap retrieves the greatest item first.
rules: pop_front, pop_back, and heap pop return Option. VecDeque uses a ring buffer and may occupy two slices.
BinaryHeap requires Ord and is a max-heap. Wrap values in std::cmp::Reverse for minimum-first behavior.
Iterating a heap does not yield sorted priority order; repeated pop does.

title: Comparison & sorting
summary: Ordering represents Less, Equal, or Greater; sorting may use natural order, keys, or a comparator.
rules: Ord supplies a total order. PartialOrd may not compare some values; floating-point NaN is an example.
sort is stable; sort_unstable may reorder equal elements and avoids stable-sort allocation requirements.
Binary search requires input already sorted under the same ordering. Use total_cmp for a total floating-point order.

title: Querying iterators
summary: Iterator queries test, search, or aggregate a sequence, often stopping as soon as the answer is known.
rules: any, all, find, and position short-circuit and advance the iterator. find returns an item; position returns its zero-based position in the remaining sequence.
count and fold consume the remaining iterator. min/max return None for empty input.
find’s predicate borrows an item while the returned result owns the yielded item; this can introduce an extra reference level for iterators of references.

title: Iterator adapters
summary: Adapters transform traversal without running it until a consumer requests items.
rules: map changes each item; filter retains matching items. flat_map expands and flattens one level.
zip stops when either input ends. enumerate attaches a zero-based counter; chain visits one iterator then the other.
take and skip depend on order in the pipeline. Peekable can inspect the next item without yielding it.

title: Fallible iteration
summary: Iterators over Result or Option can stop on the first failure instead of collecting failures as ordinary elements.
rules: collect on Result returns the first Err or all Ok values; collect on Option returns None at the first missing item.
try_for_each and try_fold short-circuit using a Try return type such as Result or Option.
filter_map(Result::ok) deliberately discards errors; it does not propagate them.

title: File operations
summary: std::fs offers whole-file helpers and File handles for streaming reads and writes.
rules: These APIs return io::Result. read_to_string also requires valid UTF-8.
File::create and fs::write truncate an existing file. OpenOptions allows explicit read, write, append, create, and truncate settings.
Import io::Read, io::Write, or io::Seek for trait methods. Dropping a file closes it; explicit flushing is needed to report some write errors.

title: Path & PathBuf
summary: Path borrows an operating-system path; PathBuf owns a mutable path buffer.
rules: Paths use platform-specific rules and may contain non-UTF-8 data; to_str returns Option<&str>.
join appends a component, but an absolute path can replace the base. components yields normalized structural parts.
Path manipulation does not access the filesystem. canonicalize resolves filesystem paths and can fail; display is intended for presentation.

title: Buffered I/O
summary: Buffers amortize small reads and writes; BufRead adds line-oriented and delimiter-based reading.
rules: lines yields io::Result<String> and strips line endings. read_line appends into an existing String; clear it between reads if reusing it.
BufWriter may hold unwritten bytes. Call flush to observe errors rather than relying on drop.
Avoid mixing buffered and direct access to the same underlying handle because buffered state can change observed positions or ordering.

title: Custom error types
summary: An error type carries failure details and normally implements Debug, Display, and std::error::Error.
rules: Display supplies a user-facing message; Error::source can expose an underlying error.
Implement From<OtherError> to enable ? to convert another error into your error type.
Box<dyn Error> can erase concrete error types. Derive helpers such as thiserror are external dependencies rather than built-in syntax.

title: Conversion trait signatures
summary: Conversion traits distinguish ownership transfer, fallible conversion, borrowed views, and text parsing.
rules: Implementing From supplies the corresponding Into implementation; TryFrom similarly supplies TryInto.
AsRef/AsMut expose inexpensive borrowed views. Borrow has stronger equality, ordering, and hashing consistency expectations.
FromStr uses type Err and fn from_str(&str) -> Result<Self, Self::Err>; parse calls it.

title: Operator traits
summary: Operator overloading implements named std::ops traits with defined method signatures.
rules: Binary traits can take a different right-hand type, such as Add<Rhs>; Output need not equal Self.
Assignment operators use separate traits with &mut self. Index/IndexMut and Deref/DerefMut support indexing and dereferencing.
Not every operator is overloadable: && and || retain built-in short-circuit behavior.

title: Drop & destruction
summary: Drop runs cleanup when an owned value is destroyed.
rules: The Drop method cannot be called directly; drop(value) consumes a value so its destructor runs.
Fields are dropped automatically after the containing value’s Drop method. Types with Drop cannot also implement Copy.
take needs Default. forget intentionally suppresses destruction and may leak resources; unsafe code cannot assume destructors always run.

title: Threads & scoped threads
summary: Threads run synchronous computations concurrently; handles allow joining and observing panics.
rules: spawn requires a Send + static closure and result; move commonly transfers owned captures into the thread.
Scoped threads may borrow local data because the scope waits for them to finish.
join returns an error if the thread panicked. Shared data requires safe synchronization; Arc alone does not make arbitrary data thread-safe.

title: Message channels
summary: std::sync::mpsc channels transfer messages from one or more senders to one receiver.
rules: send transfers ownership of the message. recv blocks until a message arrives or all senders disconnect.
channel is unbounded; sync_channel is bounded and can block sends. A zero-capacity synchronous channel rendezvous pairs sender and receiver.
Standard mpsc receive operations block an OS thread. Use runtime-specific async channels when blocking would stall an executor.

title: Atomic operations & ordering
summary: Atomic types provide indivisible operations on supported scalar values.
rules: Relaxed provides atomicity without ordering other memory. Release publishes prior writes; a matching Acquire can observe them.
SeqCst adds a single global order for sequentially consistent operations. AcqRel combines acquire and release effects where permitted.
Loads cannot use Release/AcqRel; stores cannot use Acquire/AcqRel. compare_exchange has separate success/failure orderings; failure cannot use Release/AcqRel.

title: One-time initialization
summary: OnceLock and LazyLock initialize shared state once; OnceCell is the single-threaded counterpart of OnceLock.
rules: OnceLock permits setting or computing a value once; get returns None until initialization finishes.
LazyLock stores an initializer and runs it on first access. Thread-safe wrappers require appropriate Send/Sync bounds.
Reentrant initialization can deadlock or panic depending on the primitive; avoid initialization cycles.

title: Cow: clone on write
summary: Cow carries either borrowed data or an owned form and allocates ownership only when needed.
rules: Cow<B> uses B: ToOwned; str owns as String and [T] typically owns as Vec<T>.
to_mut clones a borrowed value before mutation but reuses an existing owned value. into_owned similarly clones only when borrowed.
Use Cow when an operation can often return the input unchanged but sometimes needs to produce new storage.

title: Weak ownership handles
summary: Weak refers to an Rc/Arc allocation without keeping the contained value alive.
rules: upgrade returns None after the last strong owner is gone. A weak handle keeps allocation bookkeeping alive, not the value.
Use weak back-links to avoid strong-reference cycles.
Rc::Weak is single-threaded; Arc::Weak follows Arc’s thread-safety bounds.

title: Declarative & procedural macros
summary: Macros expand syntax before normal type checking; macro_rules defines pattern-based expansion.
rules: Fragment specifiers include expr, ty, pat, ident, path, item, and tt. Repetition uses *, +, or ? with optional separators.
Declarative macros have hygienic name resolution; use $crate for paths into the defining crate.
Procedural macros are function-like, derive, or attribute macros defined in proc-macro crates. Accepted expr/pat fragments depend on the macro definition’s edition.

title: Attributes & conditional compilation
summary: Attributes attach metadata or compiler directives to items and other supported syntax.
rules: #[...] is an outer attribute on the following construct; #![...] applies inside its containing crate or module.
cfg removes code when a condition is false; cfg! produces a bool and does not prevent its surrounding code from being type-checked.
Cargo features are declared in Cargo.toml. In edition 2024, unsafe attributes such as no_mangle must use #[unsafe(no_mangle)].

title: Const generic parameters
summary: Const generics parameterize a type or function by a compile-time value, often an array length.
rules: Stable const parameters use integers, bool, or char. A lifetime or arbitrary type is not a const-parameter type.
Braces delimit nontrivial const expressions in generic arguments. Inference often derives N from an array type.
General arithmetic on generic parameters in array lengths is restricted on stable Rust; do not assume [T; N + 1] is supported.

title: Expressions & operators
summary: Operators combine values with precedence rules and type-specific behavior.
rules: Parentheses override precedence. && and || short-circuit and require boolean operands.
==, !=, <, <=, >, and >= compare values. Arithmetic operators include +, -, *, /, and %; integer division truncates toward zero.
Assignment and compound assignment evaluate to (). ? propagates failure in compatible contexts; as performs a cast, and .. or ..= creates a range.

title: Bitwise operators
summary: Bitwise operations manipulate integer bit patterns; bool also supports non-short-circuit &, |, and ^.
rules: &, |, ^, and ! operate bit by bit. They differ from boolean && and ||, which short-circuit.
Signed right shift extends the sign bit; unsigned right shift inserts zeros.
Out-of-range shift counts can overflow; checked_shl/checked_shr return None. Choose explicit integer widths for masks and binary formats.

title: Blocks, statements & values
summary: A block introduces a scope and evaluates to its final expression, or () if it has none.
rules: A trailing semicolon discards an expression’s value. Local bindings and items are scoped to their block.
Blocks can be used as expressions; unsafe, async, const, and labeled blocks add specialized behavior.
A labeled block supports an early break with a value but does not iterate and cannot be a continue target.

title: Function pointers & callable traits
summary: fn types point to functions without captured state; closures use distinct anonymous types and callable traits.
rules: Function items coerce to fn pointers. Noncapturing, non-async closures can also coerce; capturing closures cannot.
Fn, FnMut, and FnOnce bounds accept callable values with different capture and invocation needs.
Pointer types can include unsafe and extern ABI qualifiers. Calling an unsafe function pointer requires an unsafe context.

title: Compile-time evaluation
summary: Const contexts evaluate supported expressions at compile time rather than during ordinary execution.
rules: Const functions may also be called at runtime; const marks what is allowed during compile-time evaluation.
Const evaluation restricts operations such as runtime I/O and many trait calls. A function must be const-callable to run in a const context.
Invalid constant arithmetic and other evaluation failures are compile errors. Inline const blocks provide a const context within runtime code.

title: Type aliases & associated types
summary: A type alias introduces another name for an existing type without creating a distinct type.
rules: Use a tuple struct newtype when you need a distinct type or separate trait behavior.
Generic aliases substitute their parameters; they are not constructors for tuple structs.
Associated types belong to trait implementations and are selected through a type and trait path. Generic associated types can take their own parameters.

title: Qualified paths & associated items
summary: Qualified paths select associated items when inference or ordinary Type::item syntax is ambiguous.
rules: Use <Type as Trait>::item to name an associated item from a specific trait implementation.
Turbofish ::<...> supplies generic arguments on expression paths; type-position paths usually use <...> directly.
The trait often must be in scope for method-call syntax. Fully qualified calls can resolve conflicts between traits with the same method name.

title: Unsafe boundaries
summary: unsafe allows specific operations whose memory-safety conditions the programmer must establish.
rules: Unsafe operations include raw-pointer dereferencing, unsafe function calls, mutable-static access, union-field reads, and implementing unsafe traits.
unsafe does not disable type checking or make arbitrary undefined behavior valid. Each operation has a safety contract.

Prefer explicit unsafe blocks even inside unsafe functions; edition 2024 warns about unsafe operations in unsafe functions without such blocks. Safe APIs must uphold their contracts for all safe callers.

title: Raw pointers
summary: Raw pointers represent addresses without borrow-checked validity guarantees.
rules: Creating or copying a raw pointer is generally safe; dereferencing it requires suitable validity, alignment, initialization, aliasing, and lifetime guarantees.
Null is allowed as a pointer value but cannot be dereferenced. as_ref treats null as None, yet non-null pointers must still satisfy its safety requirements.
read can duplicate non-Copy ownership and cause double drops if misused. write overwrites without dropping the previous value; pointer arithmetic also has allocation-boundary requirements.

title: Foreign interfaces & ABI
summary: extern specifies an ABI and declares or exports functions across language boundaries.
rules: Edition 2024 requires extern blocks to be unsafe. The declaration must match the actual foreign ABI, types, and calling contract.
repr(C) provides C-compatible field layout rules for suitable types; it does not make arbitrary Rust-owned types safe to pass across FFI.
Use C-compatible types and explicit pointer/ownership contracts. Avoid unwinding across an ABI boundary that does not permit it. Foreign symbols must be linked separately.

title: Union syntax & field access
summary: A union stores multiple possible field interpretations in overlapping storage.
rules: Initializing or assigning a union field is safe; reading a field is unsafe because Rust does not track which interpretation is valid.
Fields must use permitted non-dropping types such as Copy types or ManuallyDrop<T>.
The programmer must ensure the read field has a valid bit pattern for its type. A union is not an enum and carries no automatic discriminant.

title: Identifiers & raw identifiers
summary: Identifiers name bindings, items, fields, and other program elements.
rules: Raw identifiers use r# to access names that are keywords, with restrictions including self, Self, super, and crate.
A leading underscore suppresses some unused-binding warnings; _ alone discards a value instead of naming it.
Apostrophe-prefixed names denote lifetimes or labels, not ordinary identifiers. Keywords can change across editions; raw identifiers aid compatibility.

title: Arguments & environment
summary: std::env exposes process arguments, environment variables, and working directories.
rules: args and var require Unicode-compatible strings; args_os and var_os preserve operating-system strings.
The first argument conventionally identifies the executable. var distinguishes a missing variable from invalid Unicode.
Environment modification through set_var/remove_var is unsafe in edition 2024 because concurrent process/library access may be unsynchronized; prefer setting child-process environment via Command.

title: Standard networking APIs
summary: std::net provides blocking TCP and UDP sockets; asynchronous sockets come from external runtimes.
rules: TCP is an ordered byte stream, without message boundaries. Read and write through io::Read/io::Write and handle partial transfers.
UDP sends datagrams; packets may be lost or reordered. Receiving into a small buffer may truncate a datagram.
These operations normally block; timeouts or nonblocking mode alter behavior. Use runtime sockets in async applications to avoid blocking executor threads.

title: Web server structure
summary: Web frameworks combine routes, handlers, and a server runtime; these are library APIs rather than Rust language syntax.
rules: Add the framework and runtime dependencies with the features their APIs require. Axum uses Tokio; Actix Web provides its runtime integration.
Handlers normally return values convertible into framework responses; shared application state is registered separately.
Bind and serve can fail. Graceful shutdown, TLS, and deployment settings require explicit configuration beyond route definitions.

title: HTTP route registration
summary: Routing associates paths and HTTP methods with handlers.
rules: Axum 0.8 captures use {name}; {*name} is a wildcard. Captured values are extracted by handlers rather than automatically becoming parameters.
Method routing distinguishes GET, POST, and other HTTP methods on a path.
Nested routers, fallback handlers, and method fallbacks address subtrees and unmatched requests. Avoid conflicting path registrations.

title: JSON request & response bodies
summary: Framework JSON wrappers deserialize request bodies or serialize response values through Serde.
rules: Enable serde’s derive feature and the framework’s JSON support. Rust types define the expected JSON shape.
Invalid JSON, content types, or deserialization reject the request before normal handler processing.
JSON deserialization is not business validation. Validate field meanings and choose an appropriate status code separately.

title: Handler extractors
summary: Extractors convert request parts or bodies into typed handler inputs.
rules: Path and query types typically implement Deserialize. Extraction failures become framework rejection responses.
In Axum, an extractor that consumes the request body must be last; request-part extractors such as Path, Query, State, and headers precede it.
The request body is a stream and cannot generally be consumed independently by multiple body extractors.

title: Shared application state
summary: Application state makes services and data available to handlers across requests.
rules: Axum state normally needs Clone and Send + Sync + static bounds. Arc supports cheap sharing of an allocation.
Actix web::Data wraps shared ownership; create it outside the server factory to share one instance across workers.
Shared mutable data needs suitable synchronization. Avoid holding blocking mutex guards across await points.

title: HTTP responses & status codes
summary: Handlers convert response values into a status, headers, and body.
rules: Axum tuples can combine status, headers, and body. impl IntoResponse still represents one concrete return type; use Response to unify unlike branches.
Result<T, E> can model handler failure when both variants convert to responses; define safe public error messages.
Choose status codes and content types deliberately. Redirects and streaming bodies use dedicated response types.

title: Middleware composition
summary: Middleware wraps request handling to inspect, transform, reject, or observe requests and responses.
rules: Middleware must invoke the next service to continue handling, or return its own response to short-circuit.
Layer order and whether wrapping applies to the router or individual routes affect execution order and coverage.
Tower layers supply common Axum integrations such as tracing or timeouts; extra crates and features may be needed. Handle middleware errors using framework-compatible response conversion.

title: HTTP client with Reqwest
summary: Reqwest sends HTTP requests using a reusable client and offers asynchronous response-body helpers.
rules: Reuse Client for connection pooling. The json feature enables JSON serialization/deserialization; the types need Serialize/Deserialize.
send reports transport errors but does not itself reject HTTP error status codes. error_for_status maps 4xx/5xx responses to errors.
Configure timeouts and relevant TLS features. Response body consumption is normally one-shot; blocking APIs are separate and should not run directly on async executor threads.
